Age Disaggregation: From 5-Year Groups to Single Years

Source: vignettes/age-disaggregation.Rmd
age-disaggregation.Rmd

Overview

Many mortality data sources report rates in abridged age groups (e.g. 30–34, 35–39, …\ldots, 90+). However, actuarial applications, life-table construction, and population projections often require single-year-of-age rates. mortensor provides three disaggregation methods:

  1. Hyman + Kannisto: Monotone Hermite spline interpolation with Kannisto logistic extrapolation for old ages
  2. Natural + Gompertz: Natural cubic spline with Gompertz log-linear extrapolation
  3. GAM-based: 2D GAM smoothing across age and time, with parametric blending at the tail

Each method preserves the group-average constraint (the mean of single-year rates within each 5-year group matches the original grouped rate) and handles the open age interval (90+) using parametric mortality laws.

The disaggregate() function 

library(mortensor)
data(example_mortality)

sm  <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",
                        covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)
fc  <- forecast(cal, h = 10)
fc  <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

# Disaggregate to single years
fc_1yr <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100,
                       method = "natural_gompertz")

Parameters 

fc_1yr <- disaggregate(
  fc,
  target_ages = 30L:100L,              # single-year target ages
  method      = "natural_gompertz",    # "hyman_kannisto", "natural_gompertz", or "gam"
  width       = 5L                     # original age-group width
)

After disaggregation, the result is stored in fc_1yr$extras$mx_1yr_dt — a data.table with columns year, age, group columns, mx_point, and (if PIs were present) mx_lo95, mx_hi95, mx_median.

Method 1: Hyman + Kannisto

How it works

  1. Interior ages (30–89): Monotone Hermite spline interpolation (stats::splinefun(method = "hyman")) through age-group midpoints. The Hyman filter ensures monotonicity — rates increase with age, as expected for adult mortality.

  2. Open interval (90+): The Kannisto logistic model is fitted: μ(x)=a⋅ebx1+a⋅ebx\mu(x) = \frac{a \cdot e^{bx}}{1 + a \cdot e^{bx}} This provides a realistic deceleration of mortality increase at very old ages (the “mortality plateau”).

  3. Group-mean correction: An iterative multiplicative adjustment ensures the average of single-year rates within each 5-year group matches the original grouped rate.

fc_hk <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100,
                      method = "hyman_kannisto")

Strengths and limitations

  • Strengths: Guaranteed monotonicity; well-suited for all-cause mortality; Kannisto captures old-age deceleration
  • Limitations: Can be overly rigid for cause-specific mortality where non-monotone age patterns exist (e.g. breast cancer peaks in middle age)

Method 2: Natural + Gompertz

How it works

  1. Interior ages (30–89): Natural cubic spline (stats::splinefun(method = "natural")) through age-group midpoints. Natural splines allow non-monotone patterns, accommodating diseases with peaked age profiles.

  2. Open interval (90+): Gompertz log-linear extrapolation: logμ(x)=α+βx\log \mu(x) = \alpha + \beta x fitted to the last few age groups. This assumes exponentially increasing mortality, which is appropriate for most causes above age 80.

  3. Group-mean correction: Same iterative adjustment as Hyman+Kannisto.

fc_ng <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100,
                      method = "natural_gompertz")

Strengths and limitations

  • Strengths: Flexible for non-monotone age patterns; simpler extrapolation
  • Limitations: May produce non-monotone patterns for all-cause mortality where monotonicity is expected; Gompertz can overestimate at extreme ages

Method 3: GAM-based disaggregation

How it works

This is the most sophisticated approach, designed for forecast surfaces where temporal smoothness matters as much as age smoothness:

  1. Fit a 2D GAM: mgcv::gam() with tensor product smooths s(age,year)s(\text{age}, \text{year}) on the observed (training) data at grouped ages.

  2. Predict at single years: The GAM predicts log(mx) at single-year ages for both observed and forecast years, extrapolating smoothly.

  3. Parametric tail blend: At old ages, the GAM prediction is blended with a parametric model (Kannisto or Gompertz) using a logistic weight function: w(x)=11+e−(x−xopen)/τw(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(x - x_{\text{open}}) / \tau}} where xopenx_{\text{open}} is the open-interval midpoint and τ\tau controls the transition width.

  4. Group-mean correction: Iterative correction ensures consistency.

fc_gam <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100, method = "gam")

blend_parametric_tail() in detail

The blending function smoothly transitions from GAM-based rates to parametric rates at old ages:

# Internal function (shown for illustration)
blended <- blend_parametric_tail(
  mx_gam      = gam_predicted_rates,
  target_ages  = 30:100,
  open_mid     = 95,           # midpoint of open interval (e.g. 90+ → 95)
  tau          = 2,            # logistic blend width
  method       = "kannisto"    # or "gompertz"
)

# blended$mx_blended:    final rates
# blended$mx_param:      parametric-only rates
# blended$blend_weights: logistic weights (0 at young ages, 1 at old ages)

Strengths and limitations

  • Strengths: Temporal smoothness; handles forecasts and observations jointly; flexible tail treatment
  • Limitations: Slowest method; requires GAM fits from the smoothing stage; can be sensitive to GAM specification

Method comparison 

# Disaggregate with all three methods
fc_hk  <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100, method = "hyman_kannisto")
fc_ng  <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100, method = "natural_gompertz")
fc_gam <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100, method = "gam")

# Visual comparison
plot_disagg_comparison(
  mx_grouped  = fc$mx_point[, 1, 1],       # first forecast year, first group
  age_starts  = fc$ages,
  target_ages = 30:100,
  output_dir  = tempdir(),
  cause_short = "all"
)
Criterion Hyman+Kannisto Natural+Gompertz GAM
Monotonicity Guaranteed Not guaranteed Not guaranteed
Non-monotone patterns Cannot handle Handles well Handles well
Temporal smoothness Independent per year Independent per year Smooth across years
Old-age extrapolation Kannisto (logistic plateau) Gompertz (exponential) Blended
Speed Fast Fast Moderate
Recommended for All-cause Cause-specific Publication quality

Quality checks

check_disaggregation()

After disaggregation, validate the results:

# For each year and group, check quality
qc <- check_disaggregation(
  mx_grouped  = fc$mx_point[, 1, 1],    # grouped rates
  mx_single   = fc_ng_single_year,       # disaggregated rates
  age_starts  = fc$ages,
  target_ages = 30:100
)

cat("Max relative error:", round(qc$max_rel_error, 4), "\n")
cat("Monotone:", qc$monotone, "\n")
cat("Max jump:", round(qc$max_jump, 4), "\n")

The check verifies:

  • Group-mean consistency: The average of single-year rates within each 5-year group should match the original grouped rate (relative error < 1%)
  • Monotonicity: Whether rates increase with age (expected for all-cause; may not hold for cause-specific)
  • Smoothness: The maximum absolute jump between adjacent single-year rates (large jumps indicate interpolation artifacts)

Diagnostic plots

Profile plot 

# Show the disaggregation stages for a specific year/group
plot_disagg_profile(
  disagg      = fc_gam$extras$disagg_obj,
  mx_grouped  = fc$mx_point[, 1, 1],
  ages        = fc$ages,
  width       = 5,
  fc_year_idx = 1L,
  group_idx   = 1L,
  open_mid    = 95,
  output_dir  = tempdir(),
  cause_short = "all",
  group_label = "Male Q1"
)

This shows four stages: GAM raw → Parametric model → Blended → Final (after group-mean correction).

Smoothness heatmap 

# Heatmap of second differences |d²log(mx)/d(age)²|
plot_disagg_smoothness(
  mx_1yr_dt   = fc_ng$extras$mx_1yr_dt,
  output_dir  = tempdir(),
  cause_short = "all"
)

Large second differences indicate kinks or discontinuities in the age profile.

Temporal consistency 

# Check that disaggregated rates evolve smoothly over time
plot_disagg_temporal(
  disagg         = fc_gam$extras$disagg_obj,
  years          = sm$years,
  forecast_years = 2021:2030,
  group_idx      = 1L,
  output_dir     = tempdir(),
  cause_short    = "all",
  group_label    = "Male Q1",
  probe_ages     = c(50, 70, 85, 90, 95, 100)
)

Correction factors 

# Visualise the group-mean correction factors
plot_disagg_correction(
  disagg      = fc_gam$extras$disagg_obj,
  mx_forecast = fc$mx_point,
  ages        = fc$ages,
  fc_year_idx = 1L,
  group_idx   = 1L,
  output_dir  = tempdir(),
  cause_short = "all",
  max_age     = 100
)

Prediction intervals for disaggregated data

When the forecast has PIs (from add_pi()), disaggregate() transfers them to single-year ages using ratio scaling:

mlower1yr(x)=mpoint1yr(x)×mlower5yr(g(x))mpoint5yr(g(x)) m^{\text{1yr}}_{\text{lower}}(x) = m^{\text{1yr}}_{\text{point}}(x) \times \frac{m^{\text{5yr}}_{\text{lower}}(g(x))}{m^{\text{5yr}}_{\text{point}}(g(x))}

where g(x)g(x) maps single-year age xx to its parent 5-year group.

fc_pi   <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")
fc_1yr  <- disaggregate(fc_pi, target_ages = 30:100,
                        method = "natural_gompertz")

# The result includes PI columns
head(fc_1yr$extras$mx_1yr_dt)
#    year age      group   mx_point   mx_lo95   mx_hi95  mx_median
# 1: 2021  30   Male_Q1   0.000523  0.000412  0.000641   0.000518

Complete example 

library(mortensor)
data(example_mortality)

# Full pipeline
sm  <- smooth_mortality(example_mortality, method = "gam",
                        covid_years = c(2020L, 2021L))
cal <- calibrate(sm, holdout_frac = 0.2, ensemble = TRUE)
fc  <- forecast(cal, h = 10)
fc  <- add_pi(fc, n_sim = 500, method = "bootstrap")

# Disaggregate with recommended method for all-cause
fc_1yr <- disaggregate(fc, target_ages = 30:100,
                       method = "natural_gompertz")

# Inspect
head(fc_1yr$extras$mx_1yr_dt)

# Diagnostic plots
plot_disaggregation(
  mx_1yr_dt   = fc_1yr$extras$mx_1yr_dt,
  output_dir  = tempdir(),
  cause_label = "All causes",
  cause_short = "all"
)

# Life expectancy from single-year data
le <- life_expectancy(fc_1yr)
print(le)

# Export
export(fc_1yr, dir = "results/")

Summary

  • Three methods cover different use cases: Hyman+Kannisto for monotone all-cause mortality, Natural+Gompertz for flexible cause-specific patterns, and GAM for temporally smooth publication-quality surfaces
  • All methods enforce group-mean consistency with the original 5-year rates
  • The open age interval (90+) is handled by parametric mortality laws (Kannisto logistic or Gompertz exponential)
  • Prediction intervals transfer seamlessly to single-year ages via ratio scaling
  • Rich diagnostic plots help validate the disaggregation quality
